sections.COMMENTS:
This Composite Source straddles a section of the Umbria-Marche Apennines between the Upper Potenza River valley and Cittareale (from north to south), along the backbone of the Northern Apennines down to the Olevano-Antrodoco-Sibillini (OAS) thrust.
Historical and instrumental catalogues (Boschi et al., 2000; Gruppo di Lavoro CPTI, 2004; Pondrelli et al., 2006; Guidoboni et al., 2007) show a very dense intermediate (4.5 < Mw < 5.0) to damaging seismicity within the area. Furthermore, this source has generated numerous destructive earthquakes, including (from north to south): 23 April 1593 (Mw 5.5) Gubbio; the possibly twin earthquakes of 14 Apr 1747 (Mw 5.9) Fiuminata and 27 July 1751 (Mw 6.3) Gualdo Tadino; 30 April 1279 (Mw 6.3) Camerino, the well-known twin earthquakes that hit the areas of Colfiorito and Sellano in the Umbro-Marchigiano Apennines on 26 September and 14 October 1997 (Mw 5.8 and 5.7, respectively), and the 12 May 1730 (Mw 6.0) and 22 August 1859 (Mw 5.7) Valnerina events. The 14 February 1838 (Mw 5.6) Valnerina, 1 January 1328 (Mw 6.4) Norcia, and 14 January 1703 (Mw 6.8) Appennino Reatino earthquakes have occurred south of this source.
This Source results from the extensive studies that followed the well-known 1997 sequence, concerning both field evidence of present-day tectonic deformation and seismological data. Various investigators addressed the active tectonics and, subsequently, the seismogenic characteristics of the area, with widely divergent interpretations. On the one hand Cello et al. (1997, 1998) interpreted the observed ground ruptures as coseismic surface faulting, particularly in the Colfiorito basin. On the other hand, Basili et al. (1998) concluded that such ruptures were due to ground shaking, whereas the surface breaks found in the Sellano area could be ascribed to genuine surface faulting. Cinti et al. (1999) found a set of three parallel surface ruptures that they interpreted as being consistent the tectonic style of the area.
The strike of this source was selected based on that of the mapped structures. The estimation of the dip relies on geological and seismological data. The rake is representative of pure extension and was based on geological and seismological observations. Also the minimum and maximum depth were based on geological and seismological data. The slip rate was inferred from geological observations along adjacent structures that share the same tectonic environment with this Source.

pictures.t: Map of fault reactivations in the areas hit by the 1997 Colfiorito earthquakes
pictures.c: Sketch-map showing location of fault reactivations in the epicentral area of the first two mainshocks of the 1997 Colfiorito earthquake sequence (from Cello et al. [1998]).

pictures.t: Characteristics of the 1997 seismic sequence distribution
pictures.c: Location of 1997 mainshocks and aftershocks according to Barba and Basili [2000]. Notice that aftershocks cluster in the hangingwall of major faults (see A-A') and that their depth deepens to the NW in accordance with depth of faults (see C-C').

pictures.t: Map of historical earthquakes for the Colfiorito sector
pictures.c: Locations of historical earthquakes of the Colfiorito - Sellano area. The map also depicts the position of line 21, which is a fundamental branch of the Italian first-order geodetic levelling network. The line fortuitously crossed the epicentral area of the 1997-1998 Umbria-Marche sequence. Its 1998 relevelling supplied a detailed record of slip along the causative fault of the 26 September 1997 earthquake (from De Martini et al. [2003]).

pictures.t: Summary of the Central Apennines Fault System [CAFS]
pictures.c: Epicentral region of the 7 May 1984 earthquake and surroundings, showing trend of major normal faults and area of densest aftershock activity (from Westaway et al. [1989]).

pictures.t: Elevation changes and coseismic slip of the 1997 Colfiorito earthquakes
pictures.c: (left) Summary view of the surface projection of the causative faults of the seven largest earthquakes (Mw>5.0) of the 1997-1998 Umbria-Marche sequence, showing the spatial relationships between levelling Line 21 and the activated faults. (right) Contribution of the seven largest faults activated during the 1997-1998 Umbria-Marche sequence to the elevation changes measured along Line 21 (from De Martini et al. [2003]).
Historical and instrumental earthquakes (a), and geological sketch (b) of the central Apennines (from Vannoli et al. [2012]).
Location and parameters of the main earthquakes of the central Apennines and the associated Composite Sources (from Vannoli et al. [2012]).

pictures.t: Views on rate of activity of the faults
pictures.c: Diverse views on the rate of activity of faults of the central Apennines. Notice that individual faults are often interpreted differently by different research groups (from Vannoli et al. [2012]).

pictures.t: Seismotectonic sketch of the central Apennines
pictures.c: Synoptic view of the active faults and the seismogenic sources (DISS, version 3.1.1) of the central Apennines. Notice that the main extensional sources terminate to the northwest and to the southeast at the transverse OASL and ORL, respectively (from Vannoli et al. [2012]).

pictures.t: Comparison among InSAR models and dislocation models
pictures.c: InSAR models from normal faulting earthquakes: (a) 1997 Colfiorito, (b) 2009 L'Aquila, (c) 24 August 2016, (d) 1995 Dinar (Turkey) and conceptual dislacement models (Valensise et al. [2016])

pictures.t: Olevano-Antrodoco-Sibillini Line, seismogenic sources, and geofluids
pictures.c: Relationships between tectonics and geofluids in the inner Apennines. An alignment of thermal springs and CO2 emissions highlights the presence of the Olevano-Antrodoco-Sibillini Line (OASL), a major tectonic lineament, that plays a role in controlling the segmentation of seismogenic faults in central Italy (Vannoli et al., [2021]).
